objective_for_doctor: A 31-year-old Male patient presents to the clinic. Chief complaint: I have left side of the chest pain, upper chest pain, and swelling in one or more areas of your body.

turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

I’m here because I have left-sided upper chest pain and swelling in different areas of my body. I also feel very short of breath and it’s hard to breathe when I lie down, and I’ve had a lot of sweating with the pain.

Doctor: I’m Dr. Agent—first, when did this start, and is the chest pain sharp or pressure-like (and does it worsen with deep breaths)?  
Doctor: Do you notice any fever or cough, and is the swelling in your legs/feet or around your face/neck?

It started pretty fast—like within minutes, about a 6/10 speed. The pain feels like a tugging/tedious kind of pain in the upper left chest; it’s around 3/10 right now, and I’m not sure if it gets worse with deep breaths.  

I don’t have a fever or cough that I can tell. The swelling is mainly in my legs—right ankle, right calf, and left tibia.

Doctor: Any history of blood clots, recent long travel/immobility, surgery, smoking, or hormonal therapy—and have you noticed one leg more swollen or any calf pain/tenderness?  
Doctor: Also, can you tell me your heart rate/blood pressure if you’ve checked, and do you feel dizzy/faint or have palpitations?

I don’t have recent long travel or immobility, and no recent surgery that I know of. I don’t smoke and I’m not on hormonal therapy. I haven’t noticed one leg much more swollen than the others, but I do have swelling in the right ankle and right calf and also the left tibia.  

I haven’t checked my heart rate or blood pressure myself today. I do feel very short of breath, but I don’t think I’ve been dizzy or faint, and I can’t say about palpitations.

Doctor: I’m concerned about a possible blood clot in the lungs (pulmonary embolism) given sudden chest pain, shortness of breath, and leg swelling—next: do you have any hemoptysis (coughing blood) or recent unexplained weakness, and can you rate your shortness of breath from 0–10?  
Doctor: Also, right now can you tell me your oxygen saturation (if you have a pulse oximeter) and whether the chest pain is worse when you take a deep breath or when you press on the chest?

I’m not coughing blood, and I haven’t had any unexplained weakness that I can tell. My shortness of breath is pretty significant—about 8/10.  

I don’t have an oxygen saturation reading, and I’m not sure if the pain is worse with deep breaths. I can’t say if it gets worse when you press on the chest.

Doctor: Given the sudden chest pain with severe shortness of breath and leg swelling, I’m treating this as a possible pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise—REQUEST TEST: CT_Pulmonary_Angiography and REQUEST TEST: D-dimer, and please also tell me: do you have any tachycardia/palpitations, and is your breathing rate fast or are you getting worse quickly?  
Doctor: One more quick check: any history of cancer, known clotting disorder (or family history of clots), or recent COVID/infection?

I don’t know my heart rate, but I can say I’ve had significant sweating and the breathing feels like it’s getting worse—pretty quickly. I’m not sure about palpitations.  

I don’t have a known clotting disorder or cancer history that I’m aware of, and I don’t know about family history of clots. I haven’t had recent COVID or a recent major infection that I know of.

Doctor: I’m going to treat this as **high-risk pulmonary embolism** because your symptoms started suddenly, you have severe shortness of breath (8/10) that’s worsening quickly with sweating/diaphoresis, and you have leg swelling.  
Doctor: **REQUEST TEST: CT_Pulmonary_Angiography** (or **V/Q scan** if CT can’t be done) and **REQUEST TEST: D-dimer**, and I also want **REQUEST TEST: ECG** plus **REQUEST TEST: Troponin** and **REQUEST TEST: CBC/CMP**—right now, can you tell me if you have **new wheezing/stridor**, **fainting**, or **blue lips**, and do you feel **worse lying flat** (yes/no)?

I don’t have wheezing or stridor that I’ve noticed, and I’m not fainting right now. I haven’t noticed blue lips.  

Yes—I feel worse lying flat (I have orthopnea).

Doctor: Your “worse lying flat” (orthopnea) plus sudden severe left chest pain, rapid onset, sweating, and leg swelling keeps pulmonary embolism high on the list, but we also must rule out acute heart failure/acute coronary syndrome—REQUEST TEST: ECG, Troponin, BNP, Chest_X-Ray, and CT_Pulmonary_Angiography (or V/Q if CT not possible) now.  
Doctor: While those tests are pending, do you have any measured vital signs right now (heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate) and can you check your oxygen saturation (SpO₂) if possible?
I don’t have my measured vital signs right now—no heart rate, blood pressure, or respiratory rate that I can check. I also don’t have an oxygen saturation reading (SpO₂) from a pulse oximeter.

Doctor: I can’t confirm your vitals or oxygenation, so I’m going to treat this as a medical emergency—are you able to keep sitting upright, and do you have a way to get immediate EMS/ER care right now?  
Doctor: While you arrange that, I need one last check: do you have any neurologic symptoms (new headache, confusion, one-sided weakness) or have you fainted at any point since this began?

Yes—I can keep sitting upright. I need immediate EMS/ER care; I’m here now and can get help right away.  

No new headache or confusion, and no one-sided weakness. I haven’t fainted since this began.

Doctor: I’m diagnosing this as **high-risk pulmonary embolism** based on sudden pleuritic-type chest pain, severe rapidly worsening shortness of breath, diaphoresis, and leg swelling with orthopnea; we will proceed urgently with CT pulmonary angiography (or V/Q), ECG, troponin, CBC/CMP, and D-dimer.  
Doctor: While you’re taken to the ER, keep **upright**, avoid exertion, and tell them you need **immediate PE management** (consider anticoagulation after imaging assessment; escalation if unstable).  
DIAGNOSIS READY: High-risk Pulmonary Embolism (PE)
